reference.source: Mastocytosis and mast cell activation literature
clinicalPearls: A mast cell activation syndrome in which there is evidence of a clonal mast cell population but insufficient criteria for systemic mastocytosis
Patients have recurrent episodes of mast cell mediator release, often including anaphylaxis
Hymenoptera venom anaphylaxis with hypotension is a classic presentation
Clonality is shown by a KIT D816V mutation and/or aberrant mast cell markers, without meeting full systemic mastocytosis criteria
It is distinguished from non-clonal (idiopathic or secondary) mast cell activation syndrome by the demonstration of clonality
Management centres on mediator control, trigger avoidance and anaphylaxis preparedness
reference.pathophysiology: Monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome occupies a middle ground between mast cell activation syndrome and systemic mastocytosis. A clonal mast cell population, frequently harbouring the KIT D816V mutation, is present but the burden and features fall short of the diagnostic threshold for systemic mastocytosis. These clonal mast cells are prone to activation and mediator release, producing episodic symptoms such as flushing, hypotension and anaphylaxis, often with an identifiable trigger such as insect venom.
additionalInvestigations: Serum tryptase, including during and between episodes
KIT D816V mutation analysis (often on blood or marrow)
Bone marrow examination with mast cell immunophenotyping
Allergy and trigger evaluation, including venom testing
redFlags: Evolving features suggesting progression to systemic mastocytosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable with mediator-directed therapy and anaphylaxis management, though patients remain at risk of severe reactions and require monitoring for progression.
pitfalls: Failing to test for clonality (KIT mutation) in unexplained anaphylaxis
Not distinguishing it from full systemic mastocytosis
Overlooking venom allergy as a trigger
management: Mediator-directed therapy as the foundation, with H1 and H2 antihistamines, a mast cell stabiliser such as sodium cromoglicate and a leukotriene receptor antagonist, escalating to anti-IgE therapy with omalizumab for refractory symptoms
Identification and avoidance of triggers, notably Hymenoptera venom and other precipitants of mediator release
Anaphylaxis preparedness with an adrenaline auto-injector, a personalised emergency action plan and patient education
Venom immunotherapy for Hymenoptera venom anaphylaxis, often continued long term given the underlying clonality
Monitor serum tryptase and periodically reassess against systemic mastocytosis criteria to detect progression
Consider KIT-directed therapy and specialist mastocytosis input if the clonal disease progresses, within coordinated allergy and haematology care
